Assembly Language for Beginners: Talk to Your Computer in Its Own Language

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Every program you have ever run — your browser, your games, your operating system — eventually becomes Assembly language. It is the lowest-level programming language humans still write by hand: a thin, readable layer over the machine code your CPU actually executes. You probably will not build a web app in Assembly, but learning it teaches you how computers really work: registers, memory, the stack, and why your Python code is slow in some places and fast in others.

Assembly looks intimidating because it has no if statements, no loops, and no variables as you know them. Instead you move values between registers, add them, compare them, and jump to labels. Here is a tiny x86-64 program that exits with code 42:

That is the whole program. mov copies a value into a register, and syscall asks the operating system to do something. There is nothing hiding underneath — what you write is almost exactly what the CPU does.

Assembly is a good first low-level language because it removes the mystery. When you learn it, you stop guessing what "the stack" is: you push values onto it and pop them off yourself. You see why a function call costs something, why a buffer overflow is dangerous, and why a compiler's optimisation matters. It also makes you a better debugger in every other language, because when a program crashes you can read the disassembly instead of staring at it.

How to start: install NASM and a linker on Linux, or use an online assembler like Compiler Explorer's Assembly view. Write the exit program above, assemble it with nasm -f elf64 hello.asm && ld hello.o -o hello, run it, and check the exit code with echo $?. Then write a program that prints "Hello" using the write syscall, then one that adds two numbers. Each step takes an evening, and each one makes the machine less mysterious.

Who is it for? Students studying computer science, embedded developers, security researchers, and anyone who wants to understand performance deeply. If you only want to build websites, you do not need Assembly — but if you want to know what is really happening when your code runs, there is no better teacher.

The limits are honest: Assembly is slow to write, tied to one CPU architecture, and a 100-line program can take a day. You would never write a web app in it. Treat it as a learning tool and a specialist tool — for bootloaders, drivers, game engines' hot loops, and security research — not as your everyday language.

Your first step today: install NASM, assemble the exit program above, and get it to return 42. Then change the number, rebuild, and watch it change. You have just written a program with nothing between you and the CPU — and that feeling is worth the effort.

Posted on Nov 14 • Originally published at github.com

Autonomous AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor background agents, containerized SWE sandboxes) are increasingly given raw shell execution inside cloud VMs, Docker containers, or Tailscale-joined workstations. Left unguarded, two predictable failure modes show up fast:

To eliminate these failure modes deterministically across Linux, macOS, and Tailscale without external dependencies, I built and open-sourced StarHub Kit (v1.3.0) — a zero-dependency Python 3.9+ policy compiler and native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server certified Linux Foundation OpenSSF Best Practices Silver (#16658) with SLSA Build Level 3 provenance.

Instead of hand-maintaining brittle firewall shell scripts across OSes, a single declarative topology (profiles/topology.ai-sandbox.json) compiles into Linux nftables (inet), macOS pf anchors, Tailscale ACL HuJSON, and dual-stack iptables / ip6tables (--target all):

Every target supports non-root --dry-run preview directly to stdout, static risk auditing (starhub audit), and a built-in stdio MCP server (starhub mcp) for Claude Code, Cursor, or Windsurf:

Before publishing configs, starhub doctor --verify-public-export scans your working tree and Git history to verify zero private IPs, tailnet names, or keys leak into public commits.

PHP 8.6 for Laravel Developers: 5 Features Worth Using

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Posted on Nov 14 • Originally published at blog.shakiltech.com

PHP 8.6 ships on November 19, 2026. It’s already at the release candidate stage, so the feature list is locked. Most “what’s new” posts list every RFC. This one doesn’t. It picks the five features that will actually change how you write Laravel code, and shows each one in a Laravel context: collections, form requests, queued jobs and the query builder.

At the end there’s an upgrade checklist so you know when it’s safe to move production apps over.

This is the headline feature. You call a function with some arguments filled in, mark the rest with placeholders, and get back a closure instead of a result. ? stands for one argument; ... stands for all the remaining ones.

You’ve written this kind of closure a hundred times:

The closure keeps the original function’s parameter names and types, so static analysis and IDE autocompletion still work.

PHP 8.5 gave us |>, which passes one value through a chain of single-argument callables. Many useful functions take more than one argument, which used to force a closure into the middle of the chain. Partials fix that:

No closures, no temporary variables, reads top to bottom.

Partials work with any callable, including static methods, so Laravel’s helpers fit right in:

Verdict: you’ll use this weekly. Combined with |>, it removes most one-line closures.

clamp() keeps a value inside a range: it returns the value if it’s within bounds, otherwise the nearest bound. It replaces the min(max($value, $min), $max) pattern that’s easy to write backwards.

Capping a user-supplied page size is the classic case:

Or in a form request’s prepareForValidation(), so the rest of your code never sees an out-of-range discount:

It also works on any comparable type, including strings and DateTime objects, so you can clamp a requested report date into an allowed window.

Laravel already has Number::clamp(). It’s numbers-only. The native function is faster, handles dates, and throws a ValueError if $min is greater than $max (or either bound is NAN), which catches config mistakes early.

Verdict: small, but you’ll use it everywhere you handle request input.

Time\Duration is a readonly value object for a stopwatch-style length of time, with nanosecond precision. It has factory methods for each unit, arithmetic methods, and real comparison operators. It’s the first piece of a modernized date and time API in PHP.

Laravel config is full of bare integers where the unit lives in your head: retry_after => 90, $timeout = 120, $backoff = [1, 5, 10]. Was that seconds or milliseconds? Duration makes the unit part of the type.

Exponential backoff in a queued job reads like the math it is:

The last line is the honest part: Laravel’s APIs don’t accept Duration yet. For now you’ll convert at the boundary. Expect framework support to follow, the same way Carbon became the standard for dates.

A better fit today is timing things you log:

Verdict: use it in your own code now; watch for Laravel to adopt it.

PHP 8.6 adds a global SortDirection enum with two cases, Ascending and Descending. It’s deliberately unbacked (no 'asc'/'desc' string values), because SQL, APIs and query strings all spell sort direction differently. You map it at the boundary.

Every framework has invented its own version of this. A shared type means packages can finally agree on one. The RFC itself uses a query builder as the example.

Eloquent’s orderBy() still takes 'asc' or 'desc' today. But you can use the enum in your own API layer right now, and get type safety instead of validating strings:

In the controller, turn the query string into the enum once:

The enum is trivial to polyfill on PHP 8.1+ if a package wants to use it before dropping older versions.

Verdict: low effort now, likely high payoff once Eloquent accepts it directly.

This is the one you probably won’t write yourself, but it may matter most long term. The new Io\Poll namespace gives PHP native access to the operating system’s polling mechanisms: epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and BSD, and WSAPoll on Windows. Until now, userland PHP was stuck with the much slower stream_select().

You’ll almost never touch this in a controller. Its value is in the tools you already depend on. Laravel Reverb (WebSockets) and long-running servers under Octane sit on event loops, and event loops are built on exactly this kind of polling. The RFC’s main motivation is internal (signal handling, PHP-FPM improvements), with async libraries as the second audience.

The API is intentionally minimal in 8.6: it polls streams and nothing else. A follow-up RFC proposing timers, signals and process handles is already in draft. If it lands, building a serious event loop in pure PHP gets much easier.

Verdict: don’t refactor anything. Watch for Reverb, ReactPHP and Amp to adopt it and get faster for free.

Don’t upgrade production on release day. Run this checklist first:

Bonus feature: readonly properties can now have default values, so public readonly string $queue = 'emails'; finally compiles. Handy in DTOs and job classes.

If you only adopt one feature, make it partial function application. Paired with the pipe operator, it changes how everyday Laravel code reads. clamp() is the quickest win, Duration and SortDirection are bets on where the framework is heading, and Io\Poll is a quiet upgrade to the tools under your app.

By the end of this tutorial, you will have a Python script that pulls Italian business leads from paginegialle.it into structured rows: name, category type, phone, public email, street address, city, postal code, region and coordinates.

PagineGialle's listing pages sit behind an AWS WAF challenge on CloudFront. In our tests on 8 November 2026, plain HTTP clients passed only 2 of 25 pages from a residential EU IP and 7 of 25 from a datacenter server before hitting challenges. PagineGialle Scraper (reventadata/paginegialle-scraper) handles that fetch layer and parses the structured Schema.org data on each page.

⏱️ This takes about 10 minutes. Every sample row below comes from a live run on 14 November 2026.

You need three things before you run the script:

Install or upgrade the client and export your token:

You do not need a local browser, proxy credentials or scraping code on your machine.

You will run reventadata/paginegialle-scraper against Rome's restaurant directory (lazio/roma/ristoranti), read the returned dataset in Python, and print a two-line contact summary for each business.

Because everything lives inside the listing page's embedded JSON-LD ItemList, each page of up to 30 businesses requires only one fetch rather than 30 extra profile visits. You will also see why some rows have email: null or come back with a neighbouring town in locality, and how to handle those fields safely in Python.

The same workflow adapts to any Italian city and category — dentists in Milan, plumbers in Turin, hotels in Florence — simply by changing searchQueries.

Go to the PagineGialle Scraper page on Apify Store. The Try for free button opens the Actor in Apify Console if you want to inspect the form visually. Since we are driving it from Python, all you need is the Actor slug: reventadata/paginegialle-scraper.

To combine a short path and a full URL in one run:

Businesses found across multiple pages or queries in the same run are deduplicated by their PagineGialle id.

Save this script and run it with your APIFY_API_TOKEN set. It runs lazio/roma/ristoranti on page 1, waits for the run to finish, checks run.status, and prints each business:

The Actor sends requests one page at a time through an unblocking service with Italian egress, so starting with maxPages: 1 lets you check field coverage before running larger sweeps.

When the example run executed on 14 November 2026 for lazio/roma/ristoranti, it finished in 23.8 seconds and returned 20 rows. Here are the first four lines of output produced by the loop above:

Notice two real-world details right away: Hostaria Tor Millina has no public email (no email), and La Favola Ristorante Pizzeria has locality set to Monte Compatri even though the site returned it for lazio/roma/ristoranti.

Each dataset item contains 18 fields: id, name, type, url, telephone, email, streetAddress, locality, region, postalCode, country, latitude, longitude, hasMap, logo, searchQuery, page, and scrapedAt. Missing values stay null rather than empty strings, and country is always "IT".

Fields map directly from the page's JSON-LD ItemList: telephone and email come from the business's contactPoint entries, latitude and longitude are parsed as floats, searchQuery records which input query produced the row, page gives the listing page number, and scrapedAt holds the run's UTC ISO 8601 timestamp.

In the 20-row Rome run, 20 of 20 rows included telephone, streetAddress, postalCode, latitude, longitude, hasMap and logo, while 16 included email and 4 had email: null. Of those 16 emails, 9 used a custom domain, 6 used @gmail.com, and 1 used @icloud.com. Here is one complete row copied verbatim:

December 2026 Is Officially The End Of An Era For Avatar: The Last Airbender

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Avatar: The Last Airbender kicked off in earnest in 2005, and over 20 years later, it's still actively delighting tons of fans with new projects. In addition to a sweeping novel series featuring multiple Avatars throughout the series' history, there's also a live-action Netflix adaptation that just shipped its second season, and a full sequel film featuring Aang and Team Avatar was recently released on Paramount+.

Then there's Avatar: Seven Havens, which just wrapped its inaugural season and takes place 225 years after The Legend of Korra, the original Avatar sequel series. With Seven Havensrenewed, it's looking good for fans of the series.

Sadly, not everything lasts forever, and that includes some elements of the Avatar franchise. One project in particular is ending in December.

After three years in operation, developer Bamtang Games and publisher GameMill Entertainment have announced that Avatar: The Last Airbender - Quest for Balance will be removed from sale due to licensing agreements.

The announcement came directly through the game's Steam page:

"Hi everyone, we wanted to inform you that Avatar: The Last Airbender - Quest for Balance is soon to be leaving Steam at the end of December 2026 as our licensing agreement for the title has concluded. If you already own the game, there’s no need to worry, it will remain in your library and will continue to be fully playable. Thank you for your continued support! GameMill Entertainment"

Originally released in 2023, Quest for Balance is a puzzle-based game involving multiple characters from the Avatar universe, set to the tune of 18 chapters and one-to-two-player action.

"Team Avatar is back! Relive the epic adventure of the original Avatar: The Last Airbender series, as you play as Aang and his 8 friends to explore the most unique locations from the series, solve challenging puzzles and experience the most heart touching moments of Aang’s story.

Explore the World of Avatar and travel across the four nations through a 1-2 player co-op 18 chapter adventure. Play as 9 iconic characters including Aang, Toph, Sokka, and Katara. Unlock the Mysteries and navigate challenging puzzles using bending and the unique abilities of water, earth, fire and air; upgrade your abilities throughout the story to unleash the full potential of Avatar!

Reviews are decidedly "mostly negative" according to Steam, in case you're wondering what you're missing. Users report it takes roughly 10 hours to clear the game.

Avatar: Seven Havens is truly the future of the franchise right now, given the strong reception and renewal. Book One dropped on October 9 of this year, and it's already been a resounding success. Paramount ordered three more seasons, potentially telling a full story and ending with season four.

It's a massive win for Avatar fans everywhere, despite the complete erasure of Quest for Balance. If you really want to get in on this oddball piece of Avatar history, however, Quest for Balance is available to download and keep before that December cutoff.

Fast SSD leads to lower RAM requirements and smoother gameplay.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers an impressive visual and technical showcase. The game brings together several advanced graphics technologies, including Unreal Engine 5’s Nanite and Lumen, MegaLights, and RTX Mega Geometry for more accurate ray-traced shadows and reflections, alongside a range of upscaling and frame generation technologies.

However, today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally important role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage.

We’ll begin by examining its behavior on a high-end system with plenty of resources to spare, before moving to a more modest configuration that better represents the hardware available to the average PC gamer. This will allow us to see how much of a difference the technology makes, particularly on lower-end systems.

In an interview with Digital Foundry, The Coalition explained how they leveraged the Xbox Series S’s fast SSD to bring the dense world of Gears of War: E-Day to a memory-limited system. By effectively using the NVMe SSD as an extension of system memory, they can dynamically load and offload complex city data in real time. This approach allows the game to stream the necessary assets for each scene just in time, overcoming the console’s limited RAM.

Digital Foundry notes that the true “special sauce” lies in The Coalition’s smart data management. The team employs advanced heuristics to determine which assets are fetched from the SSD and when, carefully balancing performance. Overusing this technique could harm frame rates, so the system is tuned to swap data only when it benefits the experience.

Gears of War: E-Day also supports DirectStorage, although based on our previous testing, this alone does not always result in high SSD activity or read rates.

YouTuber Mostly Positive Reviews shared his findings in a recent post on X, where he found higher-than-usual SSD activity in Task Manager when playing the game.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Gears of War E-Day is visually very impressive, but something has to be done with how the game either compiles shaders or streams data. My 14400F is constantly sitting at 80% CPU usage, 16GB RAM is maxed out, and disk read is sitting at a constant 120 MBps, with spikes up to 500 MBps. Will test this with the 9060 XT as well. These are settings I chose to maintain 60 fps, which it does, except for the massive shader compilation stutters every so often.October 7, 2026

Based on his findings, we decided to investigate further.

Task Manager does not use a low enough polling period to measure SSD activity accurately, so we used HWInfo with the polling period set to 20 milliseconds. We tested SSD activity across all of the game’s graphics presets at 4K using DLSS Quality.

In our previous tests of games that relied heavily on the SSD, none came close to sustaining 1 GB/s of average bandwidth. The highest we recorded was 366 MB/s in Forspoken at 4K with maximum settings, while many titles stayed well under 100 MB/s. Some games did show higher peak bandwidths, but these spikes lasted only a few milliseconds. For our purposes, it’s the sustained throughput – reflected in the average bandwidth – that truly matters.

In Gears of War: E-Day at higher settings, we essentially have a steady stream of a little over 1 GB/s at all times, indicating that the disk is indeed being utilized as an extension of system memory. As you can see, peaks hit up to 3.7 GB/s of throughput.

We measured RAM usage on our high-end system to see how much the game will use across each generation of SSD tested.

The game uses a significant amount of system memory, but having the game installed on an NVMe SSD – regardless of generation – saves about 2GB of RAM. The storage technology seems to be working as expected.

Since the game’s average read bandwidth far exceeds the limits of a SATA SSD, we expect that installing the game on one would lead to visual issues – and that is exactly what we observe.

In the first comparison, textures are slow to load, which noticeably reduces image quality. In the second comparison, lighting and shadows take some time to appear. While everything eventually loads correctly, running the game on a SATA SSD does hurt immersion.

We tested the game across four generations of SSDs to evaluate any impact on performance. Using a high-end system with ample memory, we aim to determine the behavior of the storage technology on a system that is not resource-constrained. We will then compare the performance of our laptop’s internal PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with that of a SATA SSD.

On a system with sufficient memory, installing the game on a SATA SSD has no measurable performance impact. The only drawback is the aforementioned visual degradation.

Now, we focused on our lower-end system with only 16GB of DDR5.

Now we start to see the benefit of installing the game on an NVMe SSD, especially on higher settings.

Although the average frame rate remains virtually identical on both the NVMe and SATA SSDs, increasing the graphics preset impacts the 1% lows. The NVMe SSD delivers smoother frametimes, resulting in a more responsive and fluid gaming experience.

While the concept isn’t entirely new – Windows already uses virtual memory to page data to disk when physical memory is exhausted – The Coalition has fine-tuned this technology specifically for their game. Their approach ensures that the data being paged out won’t noticeably slow down gameplay as it’s read from disk. In our testing, this technology successfully reduces RAM usage when the game is installed on an NVMe SSD.

Placing the game on an NVMe SSD also enables near-instant asset loading. For systems with 16GB of RAM or less, an NVMe SSD can deliver higher 1% lows, resulting in smoother performance. With RAM prices climbing and many players using machines with 16GB – or even 8GB – of memory, it’s reasonable to wonder if other developers will adopt similar techniques. For titles striving to create visually dense, richly detailed worlds, leveraging fast storage could be a practical way to preserve their vision on lower-end systems.

Dan Mateescu is a PC enthusiast with many years of experience benchmarking PC hardware. In 2021, he started his own YouTube channel called 'Compusemble' where he benchmarks hardware in video games and the latest tech demos.

Italy fines Meta €805m over Facebook’s access to Android photos

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Italy’s privacy watchdog says Facebook’s Android app read phone galleries without proper consent. Meta has 60 days to fix it.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at a dinner with tech leaders in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 4, 2025.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805m, or about $887m. It says the Facebook app for Android accessed photos, videos and their metadata on Italian users’ phones without specific consent or proper notice.

The decision, first reported in English by Reuters, targets a gallery suggestions feature available since 2023. While users scroll Facebook, it offers photos and videos from their phone as ideas for posts.

The Garante found that Facebook asked for gallery access with one permission for the whole app. That request followed a vague prompt to enable other features. Users could not tell they were also switching on gallery suggestions.

Meta’s EU base is in Ireland, and under GDPR the Irish regulator usually leads. Meta argued the case belonged there. The Garante disagreed, because it acted under ePrivacy rules, which have no one-stop shop.

The rule it applied, Article 122 of Italy’s privacy code, treats a smartphone as part of a person’s private sphere. Any access to what the phone holds needs free and informed consent. It applies even if no data leaves the phone and no harm is done.

The regulator said about 20 million Android users in Italy were affected. It also weighed a 2019 decision against Meta and what it called poor cooperation. Changes Meta made after the complaint counted in its favour, but the Garante called them late and limited to users who update the app.

The fine equals about 0.47% of Meta’s global turnover. Within 60 days, Meta must ask for separate, specific consent for the feature. It must also keep the feature off by default, even for users who already granted access.

The probe did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI, which Meta denies. The Garante will look separately at a cloud processing feature launched in 2026.

The penalty is close to the €825m Dutch fine on Uber, though below Meta’s €1.2bn GDPR fine over data transfers. Meta is also tangling with Italy over a ruling on publisher payments.

Reuters said Meta was not immediately available for comment.

Dems descend on Denver to size up 2028. We asked who wants in the race

At the "What’s Next" gathering in Denver, Democratic leaders weighed the party’s future and whether they could see themselves in the 2028 presidential race.

DENVER — Democrats are already making their case for 2028.

Fresh off sweeping midterm victories, party leaders and rising stars descended on Denver for the "What’s Next" conference. Several potential presidential contenders tested their 2028 messaging before a crowd of activists, strategists and operatives.

The conversations offered an early look at who may be considering a run and who is already stepping aside.

Less than 24 hours after announcing a challenge to longtime Senate Democratic leader Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., told reporters he was "no longer pursuing" a presidential bid.

SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED

"I believe that the size and scale of these majorities, provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people," Van Hollen told reporters in Denver, as he pointed what will be at least a 55-seat Democratic majority in the chamber.

Van Hollen’s comments came as Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., weighed whether to make another run for the White House in 2028.

Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., is among the Democratic figures drawing attention as the party begins looking toward 2028. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

Booker said he is giving "a lot of hard thought" to a potential 2028 presidential campaign, though he said his focus now is pushing for what he called an "American renewal."

"My purpose right now, I want to see America in the next five years have the biggest renewal, the biggest resetting of the economic table so it works for all Americans," Booker told Fox News Digital.

He pointed to the cost of housing, healthcare and childcare as evidence that many Americans are struggling to get ahead. "The gap I’m concerned about is not the gap between left and right anymore, it’s a gap between the American people and the American dream, and I want to see that gap close," he said.

Asked what he might do differently if he ran again after his unsuccessful 2020 campaign, Booker said candidates should be "their authentic self." He also warned that political divisions are pulling the country apart, saying, "We are not each other’s enemies. We are our fellow patriots. And we all need to start pulling in the same direction."

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020, said he would have no news about a potential 2028 bid "anytime soon." (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

While Van Hollen ruled out a presidential bid, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic candidate, told reporters in Denver he would not have "any news to make about that anytime soon."

Even so, Buttigieg has not ruled out another run.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a potential 2028 contender, said he wants to be "a loud voice" in shaping the Democratic Party’s future during the "What's Next" conference in Denver, Colorado on Nov. 13, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, fresh off of major victories in his home state, said, "I've decided to be a loud voice in this process that we're going through right now as a party to put ourselves in the best position to compete."

When asked about his 2028 timeline, Shapiro said "that would be a personal decision my wife and my kids and I make."

"When we're ready to say something, we'll let you know," he added.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., told reporters in Denver she is seriously considering a 2028 presidential run during the 'What's Next' conference on Nov. 13, 2026. (Jessica Sonkin/Fox News)

Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan told reporters that she was "seriously" considering a 2028 presidential run.

"I haven't made any decisions. Whether it's me or somebody else, I just want to be a part of that next generation of leaders going forward that does things differently and understands who they serve," she added.

Pointing to a new crop of Democrats elected in the midterms, Slotkin said "we had an amazing election night that elected a whole bunch of new folks who represent that."

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said his young family will weigh heavily in his decision on whether to run for president in 2028. Gallego spoke to reporters on the sidelines of the "What's Next" conference in Denver. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

Meanwhile, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona said his young family will be a major consideration in his decision.

"I have three kids, nine, three and a one-year-old. You know, it's hard to manage that schedule and I have to figure out how to still be a good dad and run for office," he said.

"If I run I'll probably be the only one that has kids that age that doesn't necessarily come from a lot of money. So I'm going to have to figure all that out," he added.

THE MISTAKE NEWLY ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN’T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS

Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., who has not said whether he will seek the 2028 nomination, used his speech at "What's Next" to argue Democrats can build a winning coalition across the country.

"In America, all things are possible," he said, pointing to Democratic victories from New Hampshire to Mississippi.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., said he is "certainly considering" a 2028 presidential run while speaking at the "What’s Next" conference in Denver on Nov. 13, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

California Rep. Ro Khanna said he is "certainly considering" a 2028 presidential run but has not made a decision.

Khanna, one of the few leaders on the progressive left attending a conference organized by a centrist Democratic group, added "I think after the reception here, I'm, more likely to consider it. I mean, but I'm going around the country seeing whether the message will resonate."

Asked about his timetable, Khanna told Fox News Digital, "I think starting next year people will be running."

"Imagine this, we’ve had three 80-year-old presidents in a row and suddenly you’re going to have a new generation on both sides. I think that’s fantastic for this country," he said. "I'm excited about some of the people if I do run who would be competitors. It’s going to be great. It’s going to showcase America’s talent."

With no clear frontrunner in sight, the Denver conference offered an early look at Democrats testing their messages and weighing whether to seek the party’s nomination.

US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The Ukrainian president's comments come after US President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.

Russia controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.

Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Russia has now raised the stakes further. It has revived 2021 demands for Nato to halt any expansion in Russia's vicinity and to roll back military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe that became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

The US and other Western nations dismissed these demands then - and Moscow invaded Ukraine a few months later.

However, questions of European security were on the agenda of the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Russia has insisted it will not agree to cease fighting until a final peace deal is in place that would include territorial settlements as well as security arrangements.

In the comments, made on Friday but only released on Saturday, Zelensky said that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".

But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be symbolically significant for Kyiv.

Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

CoreWeave Stock Surges as Revenue Soars. Is It Too Late to Buy the Stock?

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

CoreWeave stock jumped after delivering strong revenue growth.

Neocloud stocks have seen considerable pressure this year, but CoreWeave (CRWV -6.13%) just gave investors something to cheer about when it reported its third-quarter results. The sector has been hit with a trio of headwinds in 2026, which is why it may not be a good idea to chase the current rally.

First, the group was hit with questions about how the space will finance the current build-out, especially as interest rates have begun to rise. Second, IT consultant Gartner predicted that 80% of neoclouds would cease independent operations by 2030, as artificial intelligence (AI) revenue would not support the build-out and, with high financing costs, they would not generate sufficient returns on investment. Finally, midterm elections saw many anti-data center candidates win office and quickly call for a data center moratorium and tougher permitting requirements.

Going into its earnings report, CoreWeave shares were down 32% year-to-date and 65% from their 52-week high. Let's dig into the artificial intelligence infrastructure provider's Q3 results to see whether the rally can continue or if this is a good time to sell.

CoreWeave has become one of the top neocloud providers, and that showed up in its Q3 results. The company's revenue surged 168% from $1.37 billion a year ago to $3.66 billion. That came in ahead of the $3.55 billion analyst consensus, as compiled by LSEG.

CoreWeave also raised its full-year revenue guidance, taking it to a range of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, as it expects more than 1.85 gigawatts (GW) of active power by year-end. It is projecting to end the year with run rate revenue of between $20 billion and $21 billion. The company's previous guidance was for full-year revenue of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion, with a year-end annualized revenue run rate of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion.

The company's backlog, meanwhile, rose 138% year over year to a record $132.5 billion. It currently has $9.3 billion in construction in progress and reduced its cost of debt by 250 basis points to 7.9%. CoreWeave has been working to lower its debt costs, despite higher interest rates, by paying down expensive early-stage debt and replacing it with secured loans and customer prepayments. It expects to receive $9 billion in customer prepayments within the next three months.

Importantly, CoreWeave said that it is seeing quick payback periods on its investments. On short-term contracts, it is getting a payback within six to 18 months, while on longer-term commitments, it seeing a payback in one-to-two years at current rates. It is currently getting $40 million per megawatt annually under short-term deals and $20 million to $25 million per megawatt under four- to five-year contracts.

CoreWeave also saw a nice jump in adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) in the quarter, which climbed from $838 million a year earlier to $2.26 billion. However, it continues to burn cash, and its debt continues to grow.

It generated operating cash flow of $2 billion in the quarter and $5.6 billion through the first nine months of the year. However, free cash flow was negative $7.5 billion for the quarter and negative $17.9 billion through the first nine months of 2026 thanks to $23.6 billion in capex). It ended the quarter with $67.4 billion in debt and $6.4 billion in cash and restricted cash as of Sept. 30.

CoreWeave is demonstrating that the neocloud business can work and that the returns are quite robust at current pricing. However, its growing debt load, backed by rapidly declining assets, remains a major risk, and neoclouds are highly vulnerable to construction delays stemming from the political shift following the mid-term elections. Whether short-term rates remain so robust in the future is also a considerable risk as more computing capacity comes online.

As such, I wouldn't be chasing the rally in CoreWeave or any other neoclouds, and I think that the big cloud computing stocks are the better way to play the growing infrastructure-as-a-service market.

Smart glasses could replace your monitor but they shouldn't — here's why

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Some people are already swapping their monitors for smart glasses, and the results are mixed.

Imagine taking your computer monitor and setting it out by the curb. Instead of sitting at your desk surrounded by screens, maybe all you'll need one day is a pair of smart glasses. As smart glasses ride a fresh wave of interest, some users are already experimenting to see whether the tech could be up for the challenge of replacing their monitors.

There could be some perks to using smart glasses as a replacement. For one, they're more private — no one will be peering over your shoulder. Smart glasses could also declutter your workspace and offer you more flexibility. Instead of hunching over your laptop, trying to get work done on a flight, you can use your smart glasses to look at multiple virtual monitors adjusted to your preferences.

Even so, you might not want to clear off your desk right away. From comfort issues like eye strain to display limitations, here's why smart glasses might not be ready to take the place of your computer monitor just yet.

In the life of a desk worker, there are plenty of considerations around comfort. How you sit, how you hold your head and how often you take breaks from the screen can all contribute to issues like back pain or headaches. Those who have replaced their monitors with smart glasses have encountered some sticking points as well.

An article from Lifehacker's Stephen Johnson noted that his Xreal One Pro glasses heated up when he used them for long periods, and he could feel the heat on his forehead. Different models of glasses may deal with the dissipation of heat in different ways.

On the flip side, YouTuber Jasmine Uniza said in a video that her smart glasses were comfortable, though she mostly wears them for about an hour and a half to two hours at a time. She also felt that her posture improved because she was adjusting the virtual screen to her body rather than adjusting her body to the screen sitting on her desk.

Some have also noted that eye strain could be an issue. Johnson joked that he was ignoring the old warning not to sit too close to the TV, with a screen about half an inch from his eyes. Eye strain occurs when your eyes get tired from exposure to bright lights or screens, or from focusing intently on something for a while. While it usually isn't serious and usually goes away with rest, it can be annoying.

Various testers also noted that your mileage will vary with display and resolution. Cheaper glasses might not offer a sharp enough resolution, making it harder to read text or do more precise work.

Aside from physical discomfort, some users have commented on the awkwardness of sitting on video calls wearing dark lenses or the potentially isolating effect of having glasses on at work. Others have said it was hard to switch activities because they had to take off the glasses or look past them. Writing in a physical notebook, for example, became more complicated.

Several accounts from people testing whether they can replace their monitors suggested that the glasses might be better suited to entertainment, like gaming and watching movies, than office work. Watching a movie by yourself on your couch, for example, will likely bypass the challenges of switching tasks, wearing the glasses for eight hours a day or hopping on a Zoom call with a bunch of coworkers who are wondering why you're wearing sunglasses indoors.

Smart glasses have come a long way, becoming lighter and more streamlined over time. For now they suit movie night better than the workday, but they could eventually make monitors obsolete.

MercadoLibre vs. Uber Technologies: Which Consumer Network Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

MercadoLibre's 47% revenue surge stands out, but Uber's cheaper earnings multiple and steadier balance sheet make the 2027 call far closer than the growth numbers suggest.

Investors searching for high-growth platforms often find themselves choosing between regional dominance and global ubiquity. Whether MercadoLibre (MELI +1.11%) or Uber Technologies (UBER +0.83%) fits your portfolio better depends on your specific growth objectives.

MercadoLibre serves as the primary digital commerce infrastructure for Latin America, providing essential retail and fintech services. Uber connects millions of consumers with transportation and delivery options worldwide. While both operate platform-based models, they navigate different competitive landscapes and regulatory environments, making this a classic match-up for growth-oriented investors.

MercadoLibre operates a vast digital ecosystem that includes its marketplace, the Mercado Pago fintech platform, and a comprehensive logistics network. The company maintains key partnerships with major media brands like Disney+ for its loyalty program and utilizes cloud infrastructure from Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN -0.29%). It also works with card associations like Visa Inc. (V +1.30%) and Mastercard (MA +1.32%) to facilitate payment services for its millions of active users.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $38.5 billion, which represents a growth rate of approximately 47% over the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $1.9 billion during this same period. This significant growth is a result of expanding electronic commerce adoption and the rising volume of digital payments throughout the region.

The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, is nearly 1.7x. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio of 1.2x indicates its ability to cover short-term liabilities with current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $10.8 billion, providing capital to reinvest in the business among retail stocks.

Uber Technologies connects over two hundred million monthly users with mobility and delivery services through its expansive global platform. The company has established significant partnerships with Tractor Supply Company (TSCO -0.49%) and Amazon to broaden its reach into grocery and retail delivery. It also relies on third-party mapping and infrastructure software from Alphabet to ensure its services run smoothly across thousands of cities.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, Uber recorded revenue of about $56.5 billion, an increase of roughly 14% compared to the previous twelve-month period. Net income for the company reached approximately $3.5 billion during this time. These results reflect the scale of the platform as it moves toward consistent profitability and stronger bottom-line performance.

Uber maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.4x as of its December 2025 balance sheet. Its current ratio is approximately 1.1x, which measures its capacity to pay off short-term debts with its available short-term assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached about $9.8 billion, allowing the company to strengthen its financial position and explore new growth initiatives.

MercadoLibre faces intense competition from global entrants and regional rivals. It also relies on mobile platforms controlled by Apple Inc. (AAPL +0.39%) and Alphabet Inc. (GOOG -0.96%) for its app distribution. Furthermore, the company manages credit risk within its lending solutions for merchants across Latin America.

Uber Technologies operates in a crowded field against rivals like Lyft (LYFT +2.23%) and DoorDash (DASH -0.62%). The platform must also manage complex legal challenges regarding how it classifies its drivers. Additionally, inflationary pressures on fuel and labor costs may impact its ability to maintain driver supply and net revenues.

Uber appears cheaper on an earnings basis, though MercadoLibre trades at a lower multiple relative to its sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

MercadoLibre has evolved from the so-called eBay of Latin America to something more akin to a combination of Amazon and PayPal Holdings Inc. (PYPL +1.68%). In 2025, the company made large investments in its Brazilian logistics network, cut down the free-shipping threshold in Brazil in June, and nearly doubled its consumer loan book. This drove impressive growth for the company and investors, with an increasing focus on financial services over delivering goods.

Yet the immediate concern with left-of-center Luis Lula winning the Brazilian presidential election last month is that the new administration will start addressing Brazil's high government and consumer debt levels, which will keep interest rates there around their current very high levels. That's bad for a consumer-loan-focused business like MercadoLibre, and shares have been hammered this week as a result.

Long-term, however, such fears are probably overblown. In fact, in the current fiscal year, revenue is expected to jump 45% to $41.9 billion, with slightly higher free cash flow and slightly lower net income. Overall, it's a good picture for MercadoLibre.

Uber revolutionized the taxi industry when it rolled out its ride-sharing network, allowing anyone with a car to earn a side gig. Both the industry and the company have come a long way.

Uber Technologies is by far the largest player in the developing ride-share market in terms of revenue. Wall Street expects Uber's sales to increase by $6 billion from last year to $58 billion this year, bringing with it net income of $6.4 billion. But as a sign of the expenses Uber faces in expanding its business model, that would be roughly $3.6 billion less income than in 2025. In the long run, its global ride-sharing, delivery, and autonomous solutions business will make for a strong business.

There is a lot that is appealing about MercadoLibre, but it comes at a premium P/E ratio that may not be warranted given the historically lower valuation the market puts on Latin America-reliant stocks. Right now, Uber is only slightly richer than the average S&P 500 stock (which trades around 19 times forward earnings). Based on valuation, the better choice for 2027 is the ride-sharing giant, Uber.

Malaysia plans to introduce a new law requiring data center operators to disclose their AI accelerator imports and power consumption to prevent diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China and optimize the use of the country’s power infrastructure, reports Malay Mail. The authorities also plan to charge data center operators for unused electricity capacity they reserve. While the idea to use power consumption to detect potential GPU smuggling has merit, it also has flaws.

Malaysia's Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani acknowledged on Thursday that some companies had rented space in Malaysian data centers to import GPUs legally, which they then shipped abroad in smuggling operations. To prevent such practices, Malaysia's Digital Ministry is now reviewing existing legislation to determine whether local authorities can take action against entities that re-export processors subject to U.S. export bans. The minister stressed that Malaysia wants AI accelerators imported into the country to be used domestically.

The proposed legislation will require data center operators to disclose the number of GPUs they import, their power consumption (presumably nameplate power consumption), the physical locations of their facilities, and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers. The government intends to track data center operations throughout their lifetime rather than limit oversight to the project approval stage.

Meanwhile, data center operators will have to pay for all the electricity capacity they reserve, irrespective of their actual power consumption. For example, if a data center secures 100 MW of power capacity but only uses 50 MW, its operator will still have to pay for the remaining 50 MW. The measure is meant to discourage companies from reserving electricity capacity they may not need for another one to three years. As an added bonus, the measure will further discourage rerouting AI hardware to China while pretending it is used in Malaysia.

While data on power consumption could help Malaysian authorities spot suspicious discrepancies between AI GPU imports and actual data center operations, it is virtually impossible to accurately determine the number of AI accelerators deployed at a facility based on power consumption alone. For example, Nvidia's H100 and H200 SXM GPUs are rated at 700W, whereas its B200 SXM accelerators are rated at 1,000W, yet neither necessarily consumes its rated power under actual workloads.

Furthermore, without knowledge of server configurations, the power consumption of CPUs, memory, storage, and networking equipment, or the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of a particular facility, any estimates of the number of operational GPUs would be imprecise, to put it mildly. Also, there may be a considerable delay between GPU imports and their actual deployment. As a result, reliable verification would require physical inventory audits or other mechanisms to track individual processors.

Johari said that Malaysian authorities were prepared to cooperate with their U.S. counterparts and provide information about facilities that house particular GPUs upon request. However, the minister did not specify whether the new legislation would require data center operators to disclose GPU models and serial numbers, or whether authorities would conduct on-site inspections.

Malaysia has emerged as a major destination for data center investments in Southeast Asia as cloud service providers and AI infrastructure companies expand their presence in the region. To date, Malaysian authorities have approved 117 data center projects, 55 of which are already operational, according to Johari. The proliferation of local AI data centers makes Malaysia a suitable venue for rerouting restricted hardware to countries like China, as it is easier to hide a needle in a pile of needles than in a haystack.

Pokemon fans furious after lost PokePark DS game found after 20 years is sealed in PSA slab

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Pokemon fans and game preservationists are frustrated after a playable copy of the long-lost PokePark Fishing Rally DS was authenticated and sealed inside a PSA case, leaving the 20-year-old title inaccessible to most people who hoped to finally play it.

PokePark Fishing Rally DS, also known as PokePark Fishing Contest DS, was distributed through Download Play at Japan’s PokePark theme park in 2005. Copies were temporary by design, disappearing when the Nintendo DS was switched off or after 12 hours. The game was never sold at retail, making it one of the most elusive pieces of lost Pokemon media.

As first reported by IGN, collector Daniel Qudari showed the outlet a working cartridge capable of sending the game to other Nintendo DS systems through Download Play.

PSA researcher Claire Shelton reportedly played the game during a private meeting with the owner before the cartridge was submitted for authentication and encapsulation.

The discovery initially appeared to be a major breakthrough for Pokemon historians and lost media researchers. However, much of the online reaction has focused on the decision to put the cartridge in a PSA slab before its contents were publicly preserved.

Anthony, known as @KirbyCheatFurby on X, criticized the decision, writing that “instead of making it so we can all play the ROM by dumping its contents online, they got it put in a f***ing PSA case.” The post was widely shared by fans who had hoped the discovery would lead to a public ROM dump.

and instead of making it so we can all play the ROM by dumping its contents online, they got it put in a fucking PSA case https://t.co/9NNjsxBeFI

In another post, Anthony directly asked the collector to “crack that slab open and dump the ROM,” arguing that another case could be purchased after the software had been preserved.

Pokemon collectors fear fake PSA slabs after AliExpress sells custom labels and cases for any card

Long-lost Pokemon DS cartridge sells for $11,000 after resurfacing on eBay

PSA confirms FBI investigating $1 million Pokemon & trading card heist as full stolen list revealed

collector, please crack that slab open and dump the ROM.. you gotta have the cash to put it in another slab once you're done. help us out here 😭

The reaction intensified after PSA’s certification listing confirmed that the item was genuine. Anthony later shared the certification page after saying a friend initially suspected the story could be an elaborate prank involving a 3D-printed cartridge.

my friend thought that the article was ragebait and that the slab could have just been an elaborate prank with a 3D printed cart, but sadly…https://t.co/ONrAGpuhUh

The criticism is centered on access rather than the cartridge’s authenticity. PSA has presented encapsulation as a way to document and protect a unique piece of video game history, while fans and preservationists view a software dump as the more important form of preservation.

A sealed case protects the physical object, but it also means the cartridge cannot be used in a Nintendo DS unless it is removed. As of publication, no public ROM dump of the playable copy has been announced, leaving the game effectively out of reach for everyone except the owner and the small number of people who were allowed to see it privately.

Dexerto previously reported on a separate PokePark development cartridge that sold for around $11,000 after fans hoped it might finally reveal the lost game’s contents. That cartridge’s software was never publicly confirmed, making the playable discovery even more significant.

Is the Nikon D850 Really as Good as You Remember, or Is It Just Nostalgia?

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Is the Nikon D850 Really as Good as You Remember, or Is It Just Nostalgia?

I never owned a Nikon D850, although I put some miles on my D700 over the years. I did get a chance to review the D850, though, on one of my first major press trips to Bend, Oregon. This was back in the TCS TV days, and it was there that I met many of the industry professionals who I now consider good friends.

That's a good place to start, because my time with the D850 is steeped deeply in good memories and nostalgia. It got us wondering... Was this the case for everyone else too, or is this camera actually as good as we remember?

It’s quite rare to have reviewed a digital product almost ten years ago and find that it is still available today brand new. When KEH said they had a D850 to lend us, I happily agreed to revisit this legendary camera and focus more on the shooting experience than on a proper review.

The D850 wholeheartedly deserves its legendary status. It was the pinnacle of Nikon DSLR technology, combining a relatively compact chassis with a high-res 45.7-megapixel sensor. I loved composing images through the brilliantly clear viewfinder with 100% coverage and the 2.3-million-dot LCD panel with full tilt articulation.

This is an SLR that could focus quickly, track faces and subjects with 3D-tracking technology, and fire bursts up to 9 frames per second with the right grip and battery combination.

The chassis is fully weather-sealed and made out of solid magnesium, with all the controls required to customize the camera and handle difficult shooting scenarios. Professional shooters will also appreciate the dual card slots for a CFexpress Type B card and a UHS-II SD card.

This is also a bit of a hefty camera, weighing almost 35 ounces (1 kilogram) when you throw a card and battery in. Most full-frame mirrorless cameras will weigh well under this amount, although Nikon seems to like heavy cameras, with the Z8 being the most similar, in both function and weight.

Regardless, the Nikon D850 is a pleasure to shoot, and it feels like the sophisticated tool that it is. It also happens to take some incredibly high-quality images, thanks to a sensor that may have been way ahead of its time.

It's amazing to think that a sensor placed into the D850 can still outperform modern mirrorless sensors in terms of raw dynamic range. Now, to be fair, the improvement is minor, and modern sensors read out way faster than they ever did. However, the fact is that the D850 sensor easily stands shoulder to shoulder with any full-frame camera today.

When we say that sensor technology has plateaued in the last decade, this is the perfect example. The D850 has a base ISO of 64, gathering extra amounts of light when possible, and will deliver incredible dynamic range and low-light performance. If you are looking for a rugged camera that can push shadows and pull highlights to the extreme, the D850 is a perfect choice.

Considering that the D850 can be purchased brand new for much less than a Nikon Z8, and that there is also a very healthy used market where the pricing gets even better, the D850 could make real sense to a photographer who doesn't necessarily need the mirrorless advantage.

That mirrorless advantage will largely manifest in terms of video performance, autofocusing sophistication, and more compact bodies and lenses. However, this isn't to say that the D850 is particularly weak in these regards either. I don't get the ability to autofocus anywhere within the frame, but the D850's coverage is still quite plentiful.

The 3D tracking works great even for inanimate objects, and there are plenty of situations where a single focus-and-recompose technique is all you need. Video is also fairly underdeveloped in the D850, with 4K resolution being available but somewhat soft-looking. The autofocus when using Live View is also abysmal, which was the standard for almost any non-Canon DSLR at the time.

However, there is a large market of photographers who don't care about video, don't need advanced subject-tracking autofocus, and don't mind a larger camera system. You won't get IBIS, but there are plenty of optically stabilized lenses available, and I found the shutter and weight of the camera to be solid and easy to hold steady even at slower shutter speeds.

Perhaps one of the strongest reasons to consider the D850 is just the joy of using an SLR camera as a different shooting experience. I had this same enjoyable realization when shooting the Canon Digital Rebel, and that camera is nowhere close to the D850's league. Composing with a premium viewfinder and having a powerful focusing system make the DSLR experience even better, and you don't have to break the bank to do it.

For the same price as an entry-level Nikon Z5II body, the Nikon D850 would give you a lot of performance for your money, along with an arguably more enjoyable shooting experience. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Magic: The Gathering’s 5 Best and Weirdest Star Trek References

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The set has nods to some of the franchise’s silliest moments

Magic: The Gathering’s Star Trek is a love letter to the franchise. The set uses sagas to pay tribute to standout episodes like “The Inner Light” and “In the Pale Moonlight,” and it’s stuffed with cards representing legendary characters and spacecraft along with famous quotes like “Live long and prosper.” But the set also features plenty of deeper cuts, embracing the times that Star Trek was silly, controversial, and downright terrible. These are the five best references to the franchise’s worst and weirdest moments.

If you’re wondering why one version of the art for Lieutenant Commander Data shows him dressed like Sherlock Holmes, it’s because of the Star Trek: The Next Generation episode “Elementary, Dear Data.” Chief Engineer Geordi La Forge creates a holodeck program where the android Data can play detective, but finds all of the usual mystery programs are too easy. Geordi asks the computer to create a program with an adversary capable of defeating Data, which turns out to be very dangerous.

The version of Holmes’ nemesis Professor Moriarty portrayed in Adversary by Algorithm becomes aware that he exists inside a simulation and gains access to the ship’s computer. While Data and Captain Picard are able to stop him, Moriarty returns to cause trouble in the episode “Ship in a Bottle” and even makes an appearance in the sequel series Star Trek: Picard.

Humpback Whales might seem like a better fit for Magic’s upcoming aquatic-focused set Nauctis than Star Trek, but this creature is a reference to Star Trek’s silliest movie, Leonard Nimoy’s Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home. When an enormous probe begins causing catastrophic storms on Earth, Spock realizes that the spacecraft is playing humpback whale songs. The Enterprise’s former officers travel back to 1986 to save the species from extinction. This involves a lot of antics like Pavel Chekov being mistaken for a Russian spy and Dr. Leonard McCoy using future tech to cure hospital patients. The spacecraft H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship represents the stolen Klingon Bird of Prey the crew uses in the film, which is why it lets you search for a whale and Time Walk.

The blue removal spell Pongify, which turns a creature into an ape, gets a perfect reprint paying tribute to the TNG episode “Genesis,” where a flu treatment goes awry, causing everyone on the Enterprise to de-evolve. The Klingon Worf turns into an acid-spitting monster, the half-Betazoid Counselor Troi becomes an amphibian, and First Officer Will Riker and most of the other humans regress into cavemen. Thankfully, Data is able to come up with a cure to get everyone back to normal by the end of the episode.

Star Trek: Voyager did a much worse riff on the same idea in "Threshold," which is considered one of the worst episodes in the entire franchise. The crew of Voyager is stranded 70,000 light-years from Earth, and over the course of the series they try a lot of things to shorten what would be a 75-year trip home. De-evolve is a reference to “Threshold,” where helmsman Tom Paris pushes a shuttlecraft beyond the standard threshold of Warp 10 and his body begins mutating when he returns to the ship. He then kidnaps Captain Janeway, makes her undergo the same process, and takes her to a swamp planet, where the two transform into salamander-like creatures and have amphibian babies. The crew rescued them and returned them to their human forms but left their offspring behind.

Dilemmas are a major theme of this set, representing the many ethical quandaries Starfleet officers face. But none is more notorious than the one represented in Impossible Choice. In the Voyager episode “Tuvix,” the Vulcan Lieutenant Tuvok and Talaxian cook Neelix are accidentally fused together by using a transporter while carrying alien orchids. Tuvix embodies the best traits of both characters, with Neelix’s humor making Tuvok an even better advisor and tactical officer. When the Doctor discovers a way to reverse the process, Tuvix refuses since it would effectively kill him. He begs the rest of the crew to let him live, and the Doctor refuses to p the procedure himself because of his oath to do no harm. Janeway decides she wants her old crew members back and handles the separation herself. Star Trek fans have considered her a monster ever since.

Dems' California redistricting mastermind flips script after helping party win 5 GOP seats: 'Kill'

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Outgoing Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., says the GOP House delegation from his state is dropping to four or fewer seats out of 52 — less than 10% — despite 40-45% of the state’s voters being Republican, calling it pure gerrymandering.

The architect of California's Democratic-friendly redistricting plan, which helped the party flip five Republican-held House seats in November's midterm elections, is now calling on Democrats to put an end to partisan gerrymandering nationwide.

Paul Mitchell claimed in a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed published Wednesday that lawmakers should "kill partisan gerrymandering for good." His comments come after California voters approved Proposition 50 in November 2025, temporarily replacing the state's independently drawn congressional districts with a Democratic-friendly map for elections through 2030.

Mitchell acknowledged in his op-ed that Proposition 50 was designed to benefit Democrats, but defended it as a temporary response to Republican-led redistricting efforts before calling for an end to partisan mapmaking altogether.

"I wasn’t trying to do this [op-ed] to time with anyone’s efforts to do further gerrymandering," Mitchell told Fox News Digital on Thursday evening. "I always planned on doing this as soon as the election was over, and I even did a CNN interview with Elex Michaelson during the election coverage where I said that the answer needs to be to stop this redistricting war and actually fix the problem."

REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES

Gov. Gavin Newsom spoke with supporters during a rally with the United Domestic Workers of America (UDW) about the urgency of the Get Out the Vote Kick-Off on Saturday, Nov. On Saturday, November 1, 2025, in San Diego. (Nelvin C. Cepeda / The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty)

Mitchell went on to say that Prop 50 was "the right response" to Texas Republicans' redistricting push.

"Prop 50 was the right response to what Republicans in TX were doing, but recall that when TX started doing this, our approach wasn’t to just start redistricting ourselves, we did a lot of work trying to get TX to not start the redistricting wars," he told Fox News Digital. "If then someone had said "congress will be banning mid-decade redistricting" we would have been all for it. And I supported the legislation by Zoe Lofgren that would have [set up] national redistricting standards."

Mitchell argued that Republicans' midterm losses could make them more receptive to redistricting reform after years of opposing it.

"What makes now really important is that Republicans, who have opposed redistricting reform, should now realize that they lost in this war, so getting out of future wars is something maybe they would take more seriously now," he told Fox News Digital.

As for California, Mitchell believes the Proposition 50 maps will remain in place through 2030 and said the focus should be on restoring a fairer redistricting process in 2031.

He called for Congress to prohibit mid-decade redistricting but argued that such a restriction alone would not prevent partisan gerrymandering when states redraw their maps after each census.

"I think the best solution would be independent commissions in every state," he said.

The California Democratic Party touted Prop 50 as a "direct response to a Republican power grab orchestrated by President [Donald] Trump and state leaders in Texas, who redrew congressional district lines to gain five more seats in the U.S. House of Representatives."

Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom similarly claimed in a Nov. 4, 2025 social media post that Prop 50 "is about standing up to bullies like Donald Trump."

Mitchell's recent op-ed also claims that gerrymandering can erode voters’ ability "to elect the candidates they prefer."

Democrats notably succeeded in flipping all five House seats in California targeted by the party's redistricting push in the November midterm elections, the AP reported Nov. 4.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks at a "Yes On Prop 50" volunteer event at the LA Convention Center in Los Angeles, California. Voters approved the measure, which authorized temporary changes to congressional district maps. (Getty Images)

BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES

"The incoming Congress should make national redistricting a priority, establishing minimum standards for how all states draw their districts," Mitchell wrote in the opinion piece.

BAKERSFIELD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 03: A voter marks their ballot in the Kern County Elections Office on November 03, 2026 in Bakersfield, California. Americans go to the polls in consequential midterm elections, where control of the House and the Senate is at stake for the remainder of President Donald Trump's second term in office. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Mitchell serves as the vice president of Political Data Inc., a California-based bipartisan voter data firm. He is also the owner of Redistricting Partners, a Sacramento-based data consulting firm.

Mitchell, across his career, has conducted more than 100 redistrictings for states, cities, school boards and community college districts, including the State of New York Independent Redistricting Commission, the Los Angeles City Council Redistricting Commission and the Long Beach Independent Redistricting Commission, according to Redistricting Partners' website.

When asked about whether California's gerrymandered maps were necessary during a Nov. 8 interview on "California Politics 360," Mitchell said it would have been "a huge mistake" for Democrats to "sit" on their "laurels."

Following Democrats' sweeping victories in November's midterm elections, some states have floated redrawing their congressional maps ahead of the 2028 election cycle, Roll Call reported Nov. 9.

Meanwhile, outgoing Republican Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp said Nov. 4 that he would not call a special legislative session to redraw congressional maps or limit the powers of the incoming governor before his term ends in January 2027, WABE reported.

"As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state," Kemp said in a statement.

Warren Buffett Issued His Starkest Warning About the Stock Market in Years. Here's What History Says Comes Next.

📅 Nov 14, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

More volatility could be coming, but history still has promising news for investors.

There's been no shortage of market volatility over the last week. After experiencing their worst week of 2026 in early November, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.40%), Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.91%), and Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +0.10%) are rallying once again.

However, that doesn't mean that investors are in the clear. The tech industry is still struggling with volatility -- especially after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's recent ousting -- and the market is the priciest it's been in decades.

Warren Buffett has also issued a direct warning to investors who may be underestimating market risk right now, and history has both good and bad news about what's coming next.

Warren Buffett. Image source: The Motley Fool.

During Berkshire Hathaway's 2026 meeting, Buffett discussed his thoughts on the current market in an interview with CNBC. He warned that in this historically expensive market, some investors are taking on too much risk.

"I've compared the markets to a church with a casino attached," he noted, with the church representing fundamentals-based long-term investing and the casino depicting short-term buying.

[T]he casino has gotten very attractive to people," Buffett warned, adding, "that's not investing, it's not speculating, it's gambling." He emphasized, however, that "that doesn't mean that investing is terrible. It does mean that prices for an awful lot of things will look very silly."

The S&P 500 has notched more than two dozen record highs so far in 2026, but the downside to all of that growth is that some stocks are at risk of becoming overvalued.

The S&P 500 Shiller CAPE Ratio measures the S&P 500's valuation over time based on its 10-year inflation-adjusted earnings. The higher the metric climbs, the more likely the index is overvalued and due for a pullback.

While no market indicator can predict when recessions or bear markets will begin, this particular metric has a long track record of preceding downturns. In 1929, for example, it spiked just before the Great Depression began. It surged again in 1999, during the dot-com bubble. Most recently, it peaked in late 2021, just months before stocks sank into a bear market.

In 2026, this metric reached its highest level since the dot-com bubble burst -- surpassing 40 for only the second time in stock market history. While this doesn't necessarily mean a crash is imminent, it does mean the market is incredibly richly valued right now.

The market may be pricey, but that doesn't mean it's a bad time to buy. It's crucial, however, to maintain a long-term outlook.

As Buffett mentioned, not all investing is bad. While some stocks may be overvalued right now, there are still plenty of fairly priced and even undervalued stocks with plenty of room for growth.

History also proves time and again that quality stocks will thrive over time. Since 2000, for example, the S&P 500 has faced the dot-com bubble, the Great Recession, the COVID-19 crash, the 2022 bear market, and countless smaller corrections along the way. It's also up by nearly 750% in that time.

It's impossible to say where the market is headed in the near term. But if history has just one lesson for investors, it's that healthy stocks and a long-term outlook are the keys to surviving whatever volatility may be looming.
